papers.title: Bioinformatics-driven genomic surveillance and evolutionary tracking of emerging viral pathogens
papers.abstract: Emerging viral pathogens pose a persistent threat to global health, making genomic surveillance and evolutionary tracking essential public health tools. This review evaluates bioinformatics tools, pipelines, and analytical approaches for genomic surveillance, pathogen tracking, and real-time evolutionary biology, assessing the strengths, limitations, and pathogen-specific applicability of each. Using a cross-pathogen, comparative framework, we examine five case studies: SARS-CoV-2, Ebola virus, monkeypox virus (MPXV), avian influenza virus, and honeybee viruses, each requiring a tailored combination of whole-genome sequencing, multiple-sequence alignment, phylogenetic tree building, and molecular clock reconstruction to reconstruct transmission chains and evolutionary dynamics. Key tools discussed include Nextstrain, GISAID, BEAST, IQ-TREE, MEGA, and Pangolin. These approaches have driven tangible public health outcomes, from mRNA vaccine development for SARS-CoV-2 to universal vaccine design efforts for avian influenza, but their impact remains constrained by uneven access to sequencing infrastructure, expertise, and computational resources. Across all five case studies, no single pipeline performs best universally: tool and platform choice must instead be matched to each pathogen’s biology and the surveillance infrastructure available in a given setting. Strengthening this capacity globally, particularly in under-resourced regions, is critical to ensuring emerging pathogens are detected and characterized in time for an effective public health response.

papers.title: Spatially Encoded Photonic Microsphere Lens Arrays with Deterministic Hotspaces Enabling Optofluidic Surface-Enhanced Raman Scattering Chip for Dynamic Monitoring of Multiple Biomarkers.
papers.abstract: Real-time, quantitative dynamic monitoring of multiple biomarkers is urgently needed in clinical practice; however, conventional technologies are limited by cumbersome workflows and time-consuming operational procedures. Surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) offers high sensitivity and molecular fingerprinting capability, but its application in dynamic monitoring is restricted by signal instability caused by signal irreproducibility arising from stochastic hotspot analyte spatial mismatches, and an exclusive reliance on endpoint measurements that precludes kinetic information extraction. Hence, we present an optofluidic SERS chip integrating spatially encoded photonic microsphere lens arrays (SE-PMLAs) with deterministic hotspaces to overcome these limitations. Through precise integration of gold nanoparticles onto microsphere lens surfaces, each functional unit achieves cascaded photonic-plasmonic coupling among photonic nanojets, whispering-gallery modes, and localized surface plasmon resonance, with near-field feedback reinforcement that transforms random hotspots into engineered, uniform hotspaces, delivering an average enhancement factor of 2.8 × 1010 and signal uniformity with a relative standard deviation below 5%. Using spatially encoded sensing, we demonstrate single-sample, synchronous high-throughput detection of influenza A/B viruses, adenovirus, and monkeypox virus, achieving limits of detection of 0.53 pg/mL, 128.85 copies/mL, 199.56 copies/mL, and 2.7 pg/mL, respectively. Crucially, the chip's ultrastable signal output enables a kinetic quantification model based on the initial binding rate, revealed a linear correlation between analyte concentration and its initial binding rate (i.e., slope). This approach achieves rapid, high-precision dynamic monitoring within 60 to 120s while expanding the linear detection range by two orders of magnitude. Ultimately, this chip delivers a robust, minute-level point-of-care solution for real-time pathogen screening and critical disease diagnostics.

Hence, we present an optofluidic SERS chip integrating spatially encoded photonic microsphere lens arrays (SE-PMLAs) with deterministic hotspaces to overcome these limitations. Through precise integration of gold nanoparticles onto microsphere lens surfaces, each functional unit achieves cascaded photonic-plasmonic coupling among photonic nanojets, whispering-gallery modes, and localized surface plasmon resonance, with near-field feedback reinforcement that transforms random hotspots into engineered, uniform hotspaces, delivering an average enhancement factor of 2.8 × 1010 and signal uniformity with a relative standard deviation below 5%. Using spatially encoded sensing, we demonstrate single-sample, synchronous high-throughput detection of influenza A/B viruses, adenovirus, and monkeypox virus, achieving limits of detection of 0.53 pg/mL, 128.85 copies/mL, 199.56 copies/mL, and 2.7 pg/mL, respectively. Crucially, the chip's ultrastable signal output enables a kinetic quantification model based on the initial binding rate, revealed a linear correlation between analyte concentration and its initial binding rate (i.e., slope). This approach achieves rapid, high-precision dynamic monitoring within 60 to 120s while expanding the linear detection range by two orders of magnitude. Ultimately, this chip delivers a robust, minute-level point-of-care solution for real-time pathogen screening and critical disease diagnostics.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces an optofluidic surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) chip that integrates spatially encoded photonic microsphere lens arrays (SE-PMLAs) with deterministic hotspaces to enable real-time, quantitative dynamic monitoring of multiple biomarkers. The chip uses gold nanoparticles to achieve cascaded photonic-plasmonic coupling, transforming random hotspots into engineered, uniform hotspaces. It demonstrates high-throughput detection of influenza A/B viruses, adenovirus, and monkeypox virus with specific limits of detection. The ultrastable signal output allows for kinetic quantification based on initial binding rates, revealing a linear correlation between analyte concentration and binding rate. The chip offers rapid, high-precision monitoring within 60 to 120 seconds and expands the linear detection range by two orders of magnitude. The study does not report limitations or evidence strength, but it presents a novel platform for dynamic pathogen monitoring with potential applications in point-of-care diagnostics and disease surveillance.

papers.abstract_zh: 临床迫切需要对多种生物标志物进行实时、定量动态监测;然而,传统技术受到繁琐的工作流程和耗时的操作程序的限制。表面增强拉曼散射 (SERS) 具有高灵敏度和分子指纹识别能力,但其在动态监测中的应用受到信号不稳定的限制,信号不稳定是由于随机热点分析物空间不匹配引起的信号不可再现性,以及对端点测量的完全依赖,从而妨碍了动力学信息提取。因此,我们提出了一种光流控 SERS 芯片,将空间编码光子微球透镜阵列 (SE-PMLA) 与确定性热空间集成,以克服这些限制。通过将金纳米粒子精确集成到微球透镜表面,每个功能单元实现了光子纳米喷射、回音壁模式和局域表面等离子体共振之间的级联光子等离子体耦合,并通过近场反馈增强将随机热点转变为工程化的均匀热空间,提供2.8×1010的平均增强因子和相对标准偏差低于5%的信号均匀性。利用空间编码传感,我们展示了对甲型/乙型流感病毒、腺病毒和猴痘病毒的单样本同步高通量检测,检测限分别达到 0.53 pg/mL、128.85 拷贝/mL、199.56 拷贝/mL 和 2.7 pg/mL。至关重要的是,该芯片的超稳定信号输出支持基于初始结合率的动力学定量模型,揭示了分析物浓度与其初始结合率(即斜率)之间的线性相关性。该方法实现了60至120秒内的快速、高精度动态监测,同时将线性检测范围扩大了两个数量级。最终,该芯片为实时病原体筛查和危重疾病诊断提供了强大的分钟级护理解决方案。

papers.abstract: กรมควบคุมโรค ได้รับรายงานเหตุการณ์ โรค และภัยสุขภาพที่สําคัญ ผ่านโปรแกรมการตรวจสอบข่าวการระบาด กรมควบคุมโรค จากเครือข่ายงานสาธารณสุขทั่วประเทศ ดังนี้ สถานการณ์ในประเทศ 1. อาการผิดปกติเป็นกลุ่มก้อนภายหลังบริโภคผลิตภัณฑ์อาหารเสริม จํานวน 104 ราย อําเภอนาน้อย จังหวัดน่าน 2. โรคฝีดาษวานร (Mpox) เป็นกลุ่มก้อน จํานวน 3 ราย เสียชีวิต 1 ราย จังหวัดอุดรธานี 3. การประเมินความเสี่ยงโรคฝีดาษวานร (Mpox Clade Ib) ในจังหวัดอุดรธานี สถานการณ์ต่างประเทศ กัมพูชายืนยันผู้ป่วยติดเชื้อไข้หวัดนก H5N1 รายที่ 6 ในปี 2569

analysis.research_question_and_background: The supplied evidence does not report a specific research question or knowledge gap; it presents a routine weekly epidemiological surveillance summary from the Thai Department of Disease Control.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This is a weekly epidemiological surveillance report (week 40, Buddhist year 2569) from the Department of Disease Control, Thailand, compiling nationally reported disease and health events through the national public health network.
analysis.methods: The report uses the Department of Disease Control's epidemic surveillance program to collect and verify reports of important diseases and health events from the nationwide public health network; a risk assessment for Mpox Clade Ib in Udon Thani is mentioned without methodological detail.
analysis.main_results: Four key events are reported: (1) a cluster of 104 cases with abnormal symptoms after consuming food supplements in Na Noi district, Nan province; (2) an Mpox (monkeypox) cluster of 3 cases with 1 death in Udon Thani province; (3) a risk assessment for Mpox Clade Ib in Udon Thani; and (4) Cambodia's confirmation of its 6th human H5N1 avian influenza case in 2026.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The supplied evidence does not report author interpretation or stated novelty beyond the raw surveillance counts and the mention of a Clade Ib risk assessment.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide actionable surveillance data on an Mpox Clade Ib cluster with a fatal outcome in Udon Thani, a large food-supplement-associated illness cluster in Nan, and regional H5N1 activity, informing immediate public health response and risk assessment priorities.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Evidence is limited to an abstract-only surveillance summary with no methodological detail, denominator data, case definitions, or statistical analysis; the small case numbers (3 Mpox cases, 1 death) and lack of laboratory or epidemiological linkage data constrain confidence, warranting a low evidence strength assessment.

analysis.summary_en: The Thai Department of Disease Control's week 40 (2026) epidemiological surveillance report summarizes four national and international health events. Domestically, a cluster of 104 abnormal-symptom cases followed food supplement consumption in Na Noi district, Nan province. In Udon Thani province, an Mpox (monkeypox) cluster comprised 3 cases with 1 death, prompting a specific risk assessment for Mpox Clade Ib. Internationally, Cambodia confirmed its sixth human H5N1 avian influenza case of 2026. The abstract provides case counts and locations but no methodological detail, denominator data, laboratory confirmation methods, or epidemiological linkages. The Mpox Clade Ib cluster with a fatal outcome signals a need for enhanced surveillance and outbreak investigation, while the food-supplement cluster and regional H5N1 case highlight ongoing multi-hazard monitoring. Evidence strength is low due to the abstract-only format, absence of methods, and very small case numbers.

California News Mpox outbreak hits California county as health officials probe US spread By Erica Andrews Published Oct. 30, 2026, 7:03 p.m. ET 4343 Comments See more of our coverage in your search results. Make California Post a Preferred Source 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE A potentially dangerous strain of mpox has surfaced in California’s Central Valley, with health officials investigating whether the virus is spreading within the US. Four recent cases of Clade I mpox have been reported in Stanislaus County, raising fresh concerns about possible community transmission of a strain historically associated with international travel. The California Department of Public Health has confirmed two infections as Clade I, while additional testing is underway to determine whether the remaining two cases involve the same strain, according to Stanislaus County health officials. Sign up for the California Morning Report newsletter The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now. Thanks for signing up! Enter your email address Please provide a valid email. By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy. Never miss a story Check out more newsletters Advertisement 3 A colorized transmission electron micrograph shows mpox virus particles within an infected cell. BSIP/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Three of the infected individuals reported no recent international travel, while investigators are still examining the travel history of the fourth patient. The troubling discovery comes as health authorities investigate a possible shift in how the virus is spreading across the country. Advertisement Until recently, Clade I mpox infections in the US were largely associated with people who had traveled internationally. But since August 2026, health officials have identified an increasing number of cases involving patients with no recent overseas travel. That pattern suggests the virus may now be circulating within US communities, although officials have not established how the individuals in Stanislaus County contracted the infection. Still, Dr. Thea Papasozomenos, Stanislaus County’s public health officer, stressed that the threat to the broader public remains small. 3 Four recent cases of Clade I mpox have been reported in Stanislaus County, raising fresh concerns about possible community transmission. MediaNews Group via Getty Images Advertisement “While we have identified four cases in our county, we want residents to know that the risk to the general public remains low,” Papasozomenos said. “Being aware of the symptoms, getting vaccinated if at risk of exposure to mpox, and seeking medical care when needed are important ways to protect yourself and prevent the spread of mpox.” Mpox, formerly known as monkeypox, is a viral infection that can cause painful, blister-like sores and a range of flu-like symptoms, including fever, chills, swollen lymph nodes, headaches and muscle aches. California Post App: Download here! Home delivery: Sign up here! Page Six Hollywood: Sign up here! Some patients develop only a handful of lesions without experiencing other symptoms, making infections potentially harder to recognize. Advertisement Symptoms can emerge up to 21 days after exposure, and most infected people recover within two to four weeks. However, the disease can sometimes cause serious complications. There are two major types of the virus, Clade I and Clade II, both of which spread through similar forms of close contact. The virus is primarily transmitted through direct skin-to-skin contact, including intimate or sexual contact, as well as exposure to infected sores or bodily fluids. 3 Mpox is a viral infection that can cause painful, blister-like sores and a range of flu-like symptoms, including fever, chills, swollen lymph nodes, headaches and muscle aches. MediaNews Group via Getty Images Advertisement People can also become infected by sharing contaminated clothing, towels or bedding. However, officials emphasized that the mpox virus does not spread easily through everyday encounters, such as passing someone at a grocery store or sharing an office. Health authorities are urging residents at increased risk of exposure to get vaccinated with JYNNEOS, a two-dose vaccine administered approximately four weeks apart. Those who have already received their first shot are being encouraged to complete the series for better protection. Advertisement Anyone who develops unexplained sores or a suspicious rash should contact a healthcare provider about testing, which typically involves swabbing an affected lesion. 43 What do you think? Post a comment. People who suspect they have mpox should avoid close physical contact and sharing personal belongings until they receive medical guidance. Stanislaus County health officials are currently working alongside the California Department of Public Health and healthcare providers to track the infections and prevent additional cases. news.title: Russia's Mpox Clade Secrecy Blocks Global Risk Models as Third Moscow Case Hits Domodedovo - Tech Times
news.rss_summary_html: Russia's Mpox Clade Secrecy Blocks Global Risk Models as Third Moscow Case Hits Domodedovo  Tech Times
news.excerpt_original: Russia's Mpox Clade Secrecy Blocks Global Risk Models as Third Moscow Case Hits Domodedovo Tech Times
news.priority_tier_reason: 可信机构来源或已成功抓获正文
news.content_title: Russia’s Mpox Clade Secrecy Blocks Global Risk Models as Third Moscow Case Hits Domodedovo
news.content: Medical workers wearing protective equipment wait in front of the gateway to enter the red zone to treat coronavirus patients at the Spasokukotsky clinical hospital in Moscow on April 22, 2020. (Photo by Yuri KADOBNOV / AFP) YURI KADOBNOV/AFP via Getty Images A man has been confirmed positive for mpox and hospitalized at Domodedovo Hospital in Moscow Oblast — Russia's third confirmed Moscow-region case in a single month and its eighth since the 2022 outbreak . That count, however, tells only part of the story that international epidemiologists need. For two years and across all eight confirmed cases, Russia has never disclosed which mpox clade its patients carry — a gap that prevents Europe's disease surveillance architecture from assessing whether Moscow is seeding the continent with the milder strain responsible for the 2022 global outbreak or the more dangerous clade Ib that has since spread across 23 EU and EEA countries . The case was confirmed by Domodedovo Hospital's official communications channel. All patients at the facility connected to Russia's 2026 mpox cluster have been reported in satisfactory condition and receiving routine medical care. No deaths have been reported among Russia's confirmed cases. But the absence of clade data means none of those reassuring data points can be fitted into the broader picture that Europe's public health agencies are trying to build. Domodedovo Is Russia's Recurring Mpox Flashpoint The November 1, 2026 hospitalization is not an isolated event at Domodedovo. The same hospital handled Russia's first confirmed 2026 mpox case, reported on February 2, 2026, and at least one additional case in early April 2026. In October 2026, the Moscow Oblast saw five hospitalized after suspected exposure , triggering an emergency epidemiological investigation. That same month, five cases were confirmed in St. Petersburg at Botkin Hospital. Domodedovo International Airport — one of Moscow's three major commercial airports — processed 13.9 million passengers in 2025, according to airport CEO Andrei Ivanov. The airport serves direct routes from Central Asia, Southeast Asia, and Africa — the regions with the highest ongoing rates of mpox transmission. The recurrence of cases processed through the same hospital, adjacent to one of those routes' primary arrival points, is a pattern epidemiologists outside Russia cannot yet formally characterize, because Russia has not provided the case-level data that would allow them to do so. What Russia Has Never Said About Its Mpox Strain Here is the specific gap at the center of this story: mpox virus (MPXV) circulates in two major clades, each subdivided. Clade IIb drove the 2022 global outbreak, primarily through sexual contact among men who have sex with men; it is the better-understood strain, generally considered less severe. Clade Ib emerged as the dominant threat in 2024, originating in Democratic Republic Congo . The World Health Organization declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern for clade Ib on August 14, 2024 . That PHEIC ended September 5, 2025 — but clade Ib has not ended. As of October 2026, 23 EU and EEA countries have recorded clade I cases in the past 12 months, reaching 1,939 total clade I cases , with 342 cases in September 2026 alone. In hospitalized patients, clade Ib's case fatality rate below one percent is nonetheless documented as more severe than clade IIb, and its transmissibility profile outside endemic African countries is, in the words of Canada's Public Health Agency, "not yet fully understood." That phrase represents the scientific community's honest assessment of an ongoing epidemiological question. Russia's non-disclosure of clade data across all eight confirmed cases extends that uncertainty to its own territory and, by extension, to every country with a Domodedovo flight path. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control's surveillance system covers 23 EU and EEA member states. Russia is neither an EU member nor an EEA participant, so its cases are structurally excluded from ECDC reporting . ECDC cannot fill in Russia's clade blank — that can only come from Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's Federal Service for Consumer Rights Protection and Human Wellbeing, which has not provided it. "Traditional Values" as Epidemiological Strategy: What the Cases Say Back On August 19, 2024 — five days after the WHO declared its second mpox PHEIC — Rospotrebnadzor chief Anna Popova offered Russia's official posture on the threat. "In Russia with its traditional values this disease, which is an epidemic disease, is not something we need to be afraid of," Popova told Russian media . At the time, Rospotrebnadzor had confirmed three total mpox cases in Russia. The implication was clear: Russia's cultural conservatism and the predominance of heterosexual relationships would insulate the population from the outbreak driven by sexual transmission networks. Russia now has eight confirmed cases, three of them in a 30-day window in the Moscow region. None of this disproves Popova's broader point that Russia's epidemic profile differs from Western Europe's — but the cases at Domodedovo are not arising from domestic sexual transmission networks in the way the 2022 outbreak did in Western cities. They are appearing at or near an international airport serving routes from regions where both clade Ib and clade IIb are actively circulating. Without clade identification, Rospotrebnadzor cannot confirm what Popova's "traditional values" framing implicitly assumed: that the strain arriving at Domodedovo is the one that primarily spreads through sexual contact networks, rather than the one whose transmission dynamics outside Africa remain incompletely characterized. Rospotrebnadzor has described the situation as under constant control , a phrase repeated across multiple mpox communications. That assurance sits alongside the agency's documented pattern of delayed or minimized disease disclosures on other pathogens. In October 2026, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus stated "we don't yet have the full picture" of a Siberian lab worker's death from suspected plague — because Russia had not proactively notified the WHO, and WHO learned case through media . Russia's Opacity Follows a Soviet-Era Template The October 2026 plague episode is not an anomaly in Russia's disease disclosure history — it is a recent iteration of a pattern with deep roots. In 1959, a Moscow smallpox outbreak sickened 46 people and killed three before authorities acknowledged it; the incident was suppressed during the Soviet era. In 1979, an anthrax outbreak in Sverdlovsk killed at least 68 people; Soviet officials blamed contaminated meat for 13 years before the KGB origin was acknowledged after the Soviet Union's collapse. After the 1986 Chernobyl disaster, evacuation of Pripyat was delayed 36 hours as the scale of the event was withheld from the public. "The system can silence, but it's not competent enough to coordinate, so it produces contradiction," said Judy Twigg at Virginia Commonwealth University, a political science professor who has studied Russia's public health governance and the COVID-19 data integrity question. Russia's COVID-19 death reporting drew sustained scrutiny: while Russia's official pandemic death toll stood at 338,091 through late 2021, 681,100 COVID deaths were attributable to the virus over the same period in Rosstat data. The mpox clade gap is a subtler form of the same dynamic — not a contested count but a category of data that simply does not appear. Russia Has IHR Obligations — but the IHR Has No Enforcement Teeth Russia is a WHO member state and signatory to the International Health Regulations (IHR), the legally binding treaty that requires member states to notify WHO within 24 hours of events assessed under Annex 2 as potentially constituting a public health emergency of international concern. The treaty was revised after China's 2003 SARS cover-up to include verification procedures that allow WHO to seek information from member states even when they have not self-notified. Those procedures, however, come with a structural weakness that experts have described as the IHR's defining limitation. "There is no mechanism to force countries to comply or share information," according to Alexandra Phelan Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Lawrence Gostin Georgetown University, director of the WHO Center on Global Health Law, described Russia's response to the October 2026 plague case as illustrating "the good, the bad and the ugly of the IHR," adding that countries disregarding their notification duties amounts to "a blaring siren about how unprepared we are." WHO's most aggressive lever — Article 10(4), which allows sharing information with other member states if a country refuses collaboration — is a weak instrument used by WHO sparingly . In the context of mpox clade disclosure, the absence of a clade designation does not obviously violate the letter of IHR requirements, which focus on event notification rather than granular virological characterization. But it defeats the purpose: the IHR exists to enable international risk assessment, and risk assessment for mpox in 2026 requires clade data. "Timely, transparent information sharing under the regulations is needed," Tedros said in October 2026 — a statement that applies with equal force to the question of what strain is circulating in Russia's capital region. What Europe Cannot Know Because Russia Won't Say The practical consequence of Russia's clade non-disclosure is not theoretical. Public health agencies in neighboring countries — Kazakhstan, Ukraine, Georgia, the Baltic states, and others with regular Domodedovo flight connections — cannot determine whether the cases being managed at Domodedovo Hospital represent imported clade IIb arrivals (the 2022 outbreak strain, which burned through and largely subsided in non-endemic settings) or clade Ib (the ongoing European outbreak strain, still actively circulating in 23 EU and EEA countries as of fall 2026). Those two scenarios call for different surveillance postures, different communication strategies, and different assessment of risk for travelers. The ECDC's clade I risk assessment for October 2026 rated the threat as moderate for gbMSM in EU and EEA countries, with ongoing community transmission. That assessment was built on data from the 23 countries inside ECDC's reporting architecture. Russia's cases did not contribute to it. When a traveler flies from Domodedovo to Warsaw, Vienna, or Helsinki, the risk model that public health authority is working from has a Russia-shaped hole in it. What Travelers Through Domodedovo Should Know Mpox transmits through direct contact with infectious skin lesions, bodily fluids, or respiratory particles, and through contact with contaminated personal items . It is not spread casually through brief airborne exposure in transit — an infected traveler sitting in an airport departure lounge does not pose the same risk as one with whom another person has close sustained contact. The practical risk to a transit passenger moving through Domodedovo is low. That said, travelers with upcoming Domodedovo connections, particularly those with immunocompromising conditions or those who are unvaccinated against smallpox and its relatives, should be aware of the signs of mpox infection: fever, muscle aches, and swollen lymph nodes followed by a distinctive rash that may appear on the face, hands, chest, or genitals within one to five days of symptom onset. Those who develop these symptoms within three weeks of travel through an affected region should contact a healthcare provider and disclose their travel history rather than presenting to an emergency room without warning. MVA-BN (marketed in the U.S. as Jynneos), the mpox vaccine, is authorized for pre-exposure prophylaxis in high-risk individuals. Travelers who believe they have a specific elevated risk exposure profile — including those who recently had skin-to-skin contact with someone who later tested positive — can discuss post-exposure vaccination with a healthcare provider. Russia Has Not Disclosed Clade. That Is the Story. Russia's mpox response has followed an internally consistent logic: confirm enough cases to demonstrate the surveillance system functions, keep case counts low enough to avoid triggering international scrutiny, invoke cultural framing to explain why the epidemiological threat is limited, and withhold the virological detail — clade — that would allow anyone outside Russia to independently assess whether that explanation is correct. Twigg's formulation about Russia's broader disease disclosure posture applies directly: the system silences the detail that would allow contradiction. Rospotrebnadzor knows what clade its patients carry — Vector Center, Russia's state virology institute with BSL-4 capacity, has the sequencing capability. The absence of clade disclosure from Russia's public communications is not a technical limitation. It is a decision. That decision leaves a gap in the European mpox surveillance picture that will persist until Russia changes course or the WHO finds a lever more effective than the one it currently holds. In the meantime, international epidemiologists are modeling clade Ib's spread across a continent whose eastern boundary, for these purposes, does not include Russia. Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between mpox clade Ib and clade IIb, and why does it matter for Russia's cases? Mpox virus circulates in two major clades: Clade I (further divided into Ia and Ib) originated in Central Africa and is associated with greater severity; Clade II (including IIb) is associated with the 2022 global outbreak that primarily spread through sexual networks among men who have sex with men. Clade Ib became the WHO's second Public Health Emergency of International Concern in August 2024, and as of fall 2026 is active in 23 EU and EEA countries . Clade Ib is more severe than clade IIb, though the case fatality rate in hospitalized patients is below one percent for both. The critical issue with Russia's non-disclosure is that these two clades call for different public health responses: clade IIb is well-characterized, relatively well-contained, and primarily associated with specific sexual transmission networks; clade Ib's transmission dynamics outside endemic African countries remain, per Canada's Public Health Agency , "not yet fully understood." Without Russia disclosing which strain its patients carry, neighboring countries cannot calibrate their surveillance posture appropriately. How many mpox cases has Russia officially confirmed, and has clade ever been disclosed? Russia has officially confirmed eight mpox cases since the 2022 global outbreak, according to regional reporting and health agency data . Three of these cases were confirmed in October and November 2026, all in the Moscow region. No Russian health authority communication reviewed for this article has disclosed the mpox clade for any of the eight cases. The agency's most prominent public statement on the matter — Rospotrebnadzor chief Anna Popova's August 2024 invocation of Russia's "traditional values" as protection against the disease — addressed transmission risk framing rather than virological characterization, as documented in Anna Popova's August 2024 statement . Is Russia required to report mpox clade information to the WHO? Russia is a WHO member state and signatory to the International Health Regulations, which require notification of events that may constitute international public health emergencies. news.content_original: Medical workers wearing protective equipment wait in front of the gateway to enter the red zone to treat coronavirus patients at the Spasokukotsky clinical hospital in Moscow on April 22, 2020. (Photo by Yuri KADOBNOV / AFP) YURI KADOBNOV/AFP via Getty Images A man has been confirmed positive for mpox and hospitalized at Domodedovo Hospital in Moscow Oblast — Russia's third confirmed Moscow-region case in a single month and its eighth since the 2022 outbreak . That count, however, tells only part of the story that international epidemiologists need. For two years and across all eight confirmed cases, Russia has never disclosed which mpox clade its patients carry — a gap that prevents Europe's disease surveillance architecture from assessing whether Moscow is seeding the continent with the milder strain responsible for the 2022 global outbreak or the more dangerous clade Ib that has since spread across 23 EU and EEA countries . The case was confirmed by Domodedovo Hospital's official communications channel. All patients at the facility connected to Russia's 2026 mpox cluster have been reported in satisfactory condition and receiving routine medical care. No deaths have been reported among Russia's confirmed cases. But the absence of clade data means none of those reassuring data points can be fitted into the broader picture that Europe's public health agencies are trying to build. Domodedovo Is Russia's Recurring Mpox Flashpoint The November 1, 2026 hospitalization is not an isolated event at Domodedovo. The same hospital handled Russia's first confirmed 2026 mpox case, reported on February 2, 2026, and at least one additional case in early April 2026. In October 2026, the Moscow Oblast saw five hospitalized after suspected exposure , triggering an emergency epidemiological investigation. That same month, five cases were confirmed in St. Petersburg at Botkin Hospital. Domodedovo International Airport — one of Moscow's three major commercial airports — processed 13.9 million passengers in 2025, according to airport CEO Andrei Ivanov. The airport serves direct routes from Central Asia, Southeast Asia, and Africa — the regions with the highest ongoing rates of mpox transmission. The recurrence of cases processed through the same hospital, adjacent to one of those routes' primary arrival points, is a pattern epidemiologists outside Russia cannot yet formally characterize, because Russia has not provided the case-level data that would allow them to do so. What Russia Has Never Said About Its Mpox Strain Here is the specific gap at the center of this story: mpox virus (MPXV) circulates in two major clades, each subdivided. Clade IIb drove the 2022 global outbreak, primarily through sexual contact among men who have sex with men; it is the better-understood strain, generally considered less severe. Clade Ib emerged as the dominant threat in 2024, originating in Democratic Republic Congo . The World Health Organization declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern for clade Ib on August 14, 2024 . That PHEIC ended September 5, 2025 — but clade Ib has not ended. As of October 2026, 23 EU and EEA countries have recorded clade I cases in the past 12 months, reaching 1,939 total clade I cases , with 342 cases in September 2026 alone. In hospitalized patients, clade Ib's case fatality rate below one percent is nonetheless documented as more severe than clade IIb, and its transmissibility profile outside endemic African countries is, in the words of Canada's Public Health Agency, "not yet fully understood." That phrase represents the scientific community's honest assessment of an ongoing epidemiological question. Russia's non-disclosure of clade data across all eight confirmed cases extends that uncertainty to its own territory and, by extension, to every country with a Domodedovo flight path. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control's surveillance system covers 23 EU and EEA member states. Russia is neither an EU member nor an EEA participant, so its cases are structurally excluded from ECDC reporting . ECDC cannot fill in Russia's clade blank — that can only come from Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's Federal Service for Consumer Rights Protection and Human Wellbeing, which has not provided it. "Traditional Values" as Epidemiological Strategy: What the Cases Say Back On August 19, 2024 — five days after the WHO declared its second mpox PHEIC — Rospotrebnadzor chief Anna Popova offered Russia's official posture on the threat. "In Russia with its traditional values this disease, which is an epidemic disease, is not something we need to be afraid of," Popova told Russian media . At the time, Rospotrebnadzor had confirmed three total mpox cases in Russia. The implication was clear: Russia's cultural conservatism and the predominance of heterosexual relationships would insulate the population from the outbreak driven by sexual transmission networks. Russia now has eight confirmed cases, three of them in a 30-day window in the Moscow region. None of this disproves Popova's broader point that Russia's epidemic profile differs from Western Europe's — but the cases at Domodedovo are not arising from domestic sexual transmission networks in the way the 2022 outbreak did in Western cities. They are appearing at or near an international airport serving routes from regions where both clade Ib and clade IIb are actively circulating. Without clade identification, Rospotrebnadzor cannot confirm what Popova's "traditional values" framing implicitly assumed: that the strain arriving at Domodedovo is the one that primarily spreads through sexual contact networks, rather than the one whose transmission dynamics outside Africa remain incompletely characterized. Rospotrebnadzor has described the situation as under constant control , a phrase repeated across multiple mpox communications. That assurance sits alongside the agency's documented pattern of delayed or minimized disease disclosures on other pathogens. In October 2026, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus stated "we don't yet have the full picture" of a Siberian lab worker's death from suspected plague — because Russia had not proactively notified the WHO, and WHO learned case through media . Russia's Opacity Follows a Soviet-Era Template The October 2026 plague episode is not an anomaly in Russia's disease disclosure history — it is a recent iteration of a pattern with deep roots. In 1959, a Moscow smallpox outbreak sickened 46 people and killed three before authorities acknowledged it; the incident was suppressed during the Soviet era. In 1979, an anthrax outbreak in Sverdlovsk killed at least 68 people; Soviet officials blamed contaminated meat for 13 years before the KGB origin was acknowledged after the Soviet Union's collapse. After the 1986 Chernobyl disaster, evacuation of Pripyat was delayed 36 hours as the scale of the event was withheld from the public. "The system can silence, but it's not competent enough to coordinate, so it produces contradiction," said Judy Twigg at Virginia Commonwealth University, a political science professor who has studied Russia's public health governance and the COVID-19 data integrity question. Russia's COVID-19 death reporting drew sustained scrutiny: while Russia's official pandemic death toll stood at 338,091 through late 2021, 681,100 COVID deaths were attributable to the virus over the same period in Rosstat data. The mpox clade gap is a subtler form of the same dynamic — not a contested count but a category of data that simply does not appear. Russia Has IHR Obligations — but the IHR Has No Enforcement Teeth Russia is a WHO member state and signatory to the International Health Regulations (IHR), the legally binding treaty that requires member states to notify WHO within 24 hours of events assessed under Annex 2 as potentially constituting a public health emergency of international concern. The treaty was revised after China's 2003 SARS cover-up to include verification procedures that allow WHO to seek information from member states even when they have not self-notified. Those procedures, however, come with a structural weakness that experts have described as the IHR's defining limitation. "There is no mechanism to force countries to comply or share information," according to Alexandra Phelan Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Lawrence Gostin Georgetown University, director of the WHO Center on Global Health Law, described Russia's response to the October 2026 plague case as illustrating "the good, the bad and the ugly of the IHR," adding that countries disregarding their notification duties amounts to "a blaring siren about how unprepared we are." WHO's most aggressive lever — Article 10(4), which allows sharing information with other member states if a country refuses collaboration — is a weak instrument used by WHO sparingly . In the context of mpox clade disclosure, the absence of a clade designation does not obviously violate the letter of IHR requirements, which focus on event notification rather than granular virological characterization. But it defeats the purpose: the IHR exists to enable international risk assessment, and risk assessment for mpox in 2026 requires clade data. "Timely, transparent information sharing under the regulations is needed," Tedros said in October 2026 — a statement that applies with equal force to the question of what strain is circulating in Russia's capital region. What Europe Cannot Know Because Russia Won't Say The practical consequence of Russia's clade non-disclosure is not theoretical. Public health agencies in neighboring countries — Kazakhstan, Ukraine, Georgia, the Baltic states, and others with regular Domodedovo flight connections — cannot determine whether the cases being managed at Domodedovo Hospital represent imported clade IIb arrivals (the 2022 outbreak strain, which burned through and largely subsided in non-endemic settings) or clade Ib (the ongoing European outbreak strain, still actively circulating in 23 EU and EEA countries as of fall 2026). Those two scenarios call for different surveillance postures, different communication strategies, and different assessment of risk for travelers. The ECDC's clade I risk assessment for October 2026 rated the threat as moderate for gbMSM in EU and EEA countries, with ongoing community transmission. That assessment was built on data from the 23 countries inside ECDC's reporting architecture. Russia's cases did not contribute to it. When a traveler flies from Domodedovo to Warsaw, Vienna, or Helsinki, the risk model that public health authority is working from has a Russia-shaped hole in it. What Travelers Through Domodedovo Should Know Mpox transmits through direct contact with infectious skin lesions, bodily fluids, or respiratory particles, and through contact with contaminated personal items . It is not spread casually through brief airborne exposure in transit — an infected traveler sitting in an airport departure lounge does not pose the same risk as one with whom another person has close sustained contact. The practical risk to a transit passenger moving through Domodedovo is low. That said, travelers with upcoming Domodedovo connections, particularly those with immunocompromising conditions or those who are unvaccinated against smallpox and its relatives, should be aware of the signs of mpox infection: fever, muscle aches, and swollen lymph nodes followed by a distinctive rash that may appear on the face, hands, chest, or genitals within one to five days of symptom onset. Those who develop these symptoms within three weeks of travel through an affected region should contact a healthcare provider and disclose their travel history rather than presenting to an emergency room without warning. MVA-BN (marketed in the U.S. as Jynneos), the mpox vaccine, is authorized for pre-exposure prophylaxis in high-risk individuals. Travelers who believe they have a specific elevated risk exposure profile — including those who recently had skin-to-skin contact with someone who later tested positive — can discuss post-exposure vaccination with a healthcare provider. Russia Has Not Disclosed Clade. That Is the Story. Russia's mpox response has followed an internally consistent logic: confirm enough cases to demonstrate the surveillance system functions, keep case counts low enough to avoid triggering international scrutiny, invoke cultural framing to explain why the epidemiological threat is limited, and withhold the virological detail — clade — that would allow anyone outside Russia to independently assess whether that explanation is correct. Twigg's formulation about Russia's broader disease disclosure posture applies directly: the system silences the detail that would allow contradiction. Rospotrebnadzor knows what clade its patients carry — Vector Center, Russia's state virology institute with BSL-4 capacity, has the sequencing capability. The absence of clade disclosure from Russia's public communications is not a technical limitation. It is a decision. That decision leaves a gap in the European mpox surveillance picture that will persist until Russia changes course or the WHO finds a lever more effective than the one it currently holds. In the meantime, international epidemiologists are modeling clade Ib's spread across a continent whose eastern boundary, for these purposes, does not include Russia. news.content_zh: 一名男子被确认感染猴痘病毒,并被送往莫斯科州多莫杰多沃医院住院治疗,标志着俄罗斯本月第三例确诊病例,以及自2022年暴发疫情以来的第八例确诊病例。这一病例凸显了俄罗斯疾病报告中的关键漏洞:所有八例确诊病例均未提供分支数据,这使得全球卫生机构无法判断该病毒株是否属于更严重的Ib分支,该分支已在23个欧盟和欧洲经济区国家传播,或是较轻的IIb分支,该分支与2022年的全球暴发疫情相关。多莫杰多沃医院服务于来自中亚、东南亚和非洲的国际航线,2026年已处理多起猴痘病例,包括2月份的首例确诊病例和4月初至少一例。缺乏分支数据意味着这些病例对全球健康构成的风险无法准确评估,而俄罗斯联邦消费者权益保护和人道主义事务局(Rospotrebnadzor)并未提供相关信息。世界卫生组织指出,俄罗斯的疾病报告实践仍然不透明,例如2026年10月对西伯利亚实验室工作人员疑似鼠疫死亡的延迟披露。这种保密模式并非首次出现,历史上曾有1959年天花暴发疫情被压制,以及1979年斯维尔德洛夫斯克炭疽事件的延迟承认。目前该情况仍在调查中,俄罗斯确认的病例中尚未报告死亡。
news.summary_zh: 一名男子被确认感染猴痘病毒,并被送往莫斯科州多莫杰多沃医院住院治疗,标志着俄罗斯本月第三例确诊病例,以及自2022年暴发疫情以来的第八例确诊病例。这一病例凸显了俄罗斯疾病报告中的关键漏洞:所有八例确诊病例均未提供分支数据,这使得全球卫生机构无法判断该病毒株是否属于更严重的Ib分支,该分支已在23个欧盟和欧洲经济区国家传播,或是较轻的IIb分支,该分支与2022年的全球暴发疫情相关。多莫杰多沃医院服务于来自中亚、东南亚和非洲的国际航线,2026年已处理多起猴痘病例,包括2月份的首例确诊病例和4月初至少一例。缺乏分支数据意味着这些病例对全球健康构成的风险无法准确评估,而俄罗斯联邦消费者权益保护和人道主义事务局(Rospotrebnadzor)并未提供相关信息。世界卫生组织指出,俄罗斯的疾病报告实践仍然不透明,例如2026年10月对西伯利亚实验室工作人员疑似鼠疫死亡的延迟披露。这种保密模式并非首次出现,历史上曾有1959年天花暴发疫情被压制,以及1979年斯维尔德洛夫斯克炭疽事件的延迟承认。目前该情况仍在调查中,俄罗斯确认的病例中尚未报告死亡。

analysis_zh.time: 第三例莫斯科地区猴痘病例于2026年11月1日被确认。俄罗斯2026年的首例确诊病例于2026年2月2日报告,且在2026年4月初至少报告了一例额外病例。2022年的暴发疫情被作为历史背景提及,世界卫生组织关于Ib分支的公共卫生紧急事件(PHEIC)已于2025年9月5日结束。
analysis_zh.location_and_population: 该病例发生在莫斯科州的多莫杰多沃医院。该医院位于多莫杰多沃国际机场附近,该机场提供来自中亚、东南亚和非洲的国际航线。莫斯科州和圣彼得堡已被确认为出现猴痘病例的地区,且该医院在2026年已处理多起病例。
analysis_zh.event: 一名男子被确认感染猴痘病毒,并被送往莫斯科州多莫杰多沃医院住院治疗,标志着俄罗斯在该月内第三例莫斯科地区确诊病例,以及自2022年暴发疫情以来的第八例确诊病例。该事件由多莫杰多沃医院的官方通讯渠道报告。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 截至2026年10月,23个欧盟和欧洲经济区国家共记录了1,939例Ib分支病例,其中仅2026年9月就出现了342例。Ib分支被认为比IIb分支更为严重,其记录的病例死亡率低于1%。俄罗斯未披露分支数据,阻碍了对其病例对全球健康风险的准确评估。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: Rospotrebnadzor表示该情况处于持续控制之下,但这一保证伴随着延迟或最小化疾病披露的既定模式。缺乏分支数据意味着该机构无法确认病毒株的传播动态,世界卫生组织也指出俄罗斯的疾病报告实践仍然不透明。

The Modesto Bee reports that California state health officials confirmed the two clade I cases, while Stanislaus County health officials reported all four as recent infections. Mpox, formerly known as monkeypox, is a rare viral infection that causes a painful or itchy rash along with flu-like symptoms, according to the Stanislaus County Health Services Agency. Despite the new cases, the agency said the current risk of mpox for the general public remains very low. Two Strains, Two Very Different Risk Profiles Clade I mpox may be more severe than clade II, according to KPBS, and the distinction matters because of how differently the two strains have behaved. Clade I carries a mortality rate upward of 10%, attributed to Johns Hopkins School of Public Health, while clade II carries a mortality rate of 1% to 4% by the same attribution. Clade II is the strain that spurred the global mpox outbreak in 2022. Clade I mpox cases have often been linked to international travel, though infections among people without foreign travel in the past three months have been increasing, raising concern among U.S. communities about local spread. Clade I outbreaks have been centered in Central and Eastern Africa and Western Europe. The California Department of Public Health previously confirmed three unrelated clade I cases in Long Beach and Los Angeles County in 2025, and all three of those patients were hospitalized. County Says It's Tracking the Situation Closely Stanislaus County is working with the California Department of Public Health to monitor the mpox situation, the county health agency said, as officials try to pin down the classification of the two unidentified cases. Dr. Thea Papasozomenos said the public risk remains low despite the four county cases, and advised that awareness of symptoms, vaccination for those at higher risk, and seeking medical care when needed can help protect people and prevent further spread. Nationally, the picture has been shifting. The CDC reports that nearly 130 clade I mpox cases have been reported across at least 26 states plus Puerto Rico as of October, and that imported clade I cases began increasing in frequency starting in March, with local transmission occurring since August — a pattern the agency says points to a likely transition toward sustained clade Ib transmission in the United States. A separate CDC report notes that subclade IIb transmission persists at low levels nationally, while subclade Ib has spread across roughly 40 countries and includes travel-associated cases here. What Mpox Looks Like and How It Spreads The most common symptom of mpox is lesions, according to the county health agency, though some people develop only a few skin sores without any other symptoms. Other symptoms can include a rash or sores resembling pimples or blisters, along with fever, chills, swollen lymph nodes, headache, body aches, and fatigue. The virus spreads mostly through close contact, skin-to-skin contact, or sexual activity, and it can also spread through contaminated bedding, towels, or clothes — though casual interactions are not known to spread it easily. Anyone who develops an unexplained rash or sores is urged to contact a healthcare provider to ask about mpox testing, which involves swabbing the rash or sores. People who suspect they have mpox should avoid close physical contact with others, refrain from sharing personal items, and isolate until all sores have healed and new skin has formed. Vaccine Guidance for Those at Higher Risk JYNNEOS, the vaccine available for mpox, is recommended for people at higher risk of exposure and is given in two doses four weeks apart, according to FOX5 Vegas, and it is expected to protect against both clade I and clade II infection and serious illness. The California Department of Public Health recommends vaccination for gay or bisexual men and other men who have sex with men, transgender or gender-diverse individuals, people living with HIV or taking HIV PrEP or doxy PEP, anyone exposed to mpox in the previous two weeks, and travelers heading to a country with clade I spread who anticipate sexual or intimate contact. People who have already received one dose are encouraged to complete the series, and the overall vaccination goal is increasing coverage in high-risk groups given the current outbreaks. Anyone unsure of their own risk is encouraged to discuss it with a healthcare provider. How Stanislaus County Compares to Other Regions Stanislaus County is far from alone in confronting new mpox activity this year. San Diego County reported 27 clade II cases in 2026, mostly among people who were not fully vaccinated, all involving men between 17 and 53 years old, according to KPBS. The outlet also notes that most clade I cases outside Africa are associated with travel, though some areas have reported local spread. In Nevada, the Southern Nevada Health District recently announced its first confirmed clade I case in a Clark County resident with no reported travel exposure, on top of 11 confirmed clade II cases reported since August, per the station's report. That same district has logged 365 mpox cases total in Clark County since its first case was reported back in June 2022. Separately, NEJM Evidence has documented a clade Ib outbreak across Central and Eastern Africa driving multiple travel-associated infections, including three unvaccinated people confirmed infected in October 2025. news.title_zh: 斯坦尼斯拉乌斯县报告四例猴痘病例,其中两例属于I型克隆株 - 人兽共患病
news.source_body_en: Stanislaus County, California, confirmed four mpox cases as of October 30, 2026, with two identified as the more severe clade I strain. The county health officials are collaborating with the California Department of Public Health to monitor the situation and determine the classification of the remaining two cases. While the mortality rate for clade I is upward of 10%, the risk for the general public remains very low. Health officials recommend awareness of symptoms, vaccination for high-risk individuals, and isolation for suspected cases to prevent further spread. The Modesto Bee reported that state health officials confirmed the two clade I cases, and all four infections are recent. The CDC notes that nearly 130 clade I cases have been reported across 26 states and Puerto Rico, with local transmission occurring since August. Clade II, which caused the 2022 global outbreak, continues to spread at low levels nationally. Public health guidance emphasizes avoiding close contact, refraining from sharing personal items, and seeking medical care for unexplained rashes or sores.
news.content_zh: 截至2026年10月30日,加利福尼亚州斯坦尼斯拉乌斯县确认了四例猴痘病例,其中两例被鉴定为更为严重的I型克隆株。该县卫生官员正与加利福尼亚州公共卫生部合作,监测局势并确定剩余两例病例的分类。尽管I型克隆株的死亡率率超过10%,但对一般公众的风险仍然非常低。卫生官员建议提高对症状的意识,对高风险人群进行疫苗接种,并对疑似病例采取隔离措施以防止进一步传播。据《莫德斯托蜜蜂报》报道,州卫生官员确认了两例I型克隆株病例,且所有四例感染均为近期发生。美国疾病控制与预防中心(CDC)指出,截至目前为止,全美26个州和波多黎各已报告近130例I型克隆株病例,且本地传播自8月起已发生。导致2022年全球暴发的II型克隆株在全国范围内仍以低水平持续传播。公共卫生指导建议避免密切接触,不共用个人物品,并在出现不明原因皮疹或疮口时寻求医疗帮助。

news.content: Nov 01, 06:44 pm EST Medical Daily VITALITY MENTAL HEALTH INNOVATION HEALTHY LIVING CONDITIONS Search form Search Vitality How to Live Better, Longer U.S. Men Live Nearly Five Years Less Than Women as Lancet Series Calls for Men's Health Policies A new Lancet series says men lose more healthy years than women worldwide and urges governments to address poverty, social pressures, prevention and access to care through men's health policies. HHS Refers Duke Medical School to Justice Department Over Alleged Race Use in Admissions The Department of Health and Human Services referred Duke University School of Medicine to the Justice Department, alleging race and race-related proxies influenced admissions decisions. Duke disputes the claims. Kentucky Erases $153 Million in Medical Debt for 67,000 Residents as Second-Round Relief Letters Head to Mailboxes Kentucky has canceled about $153 million in medical debt for 67,000 residents through a state-funded nonprofit program. Relief is automatic, but only eligible debts are covered. Halloween Saw 45 Child Pedestrian Deaths Over 15 Years, Nearly Double Any Other Date on the Calendar A MoneyGeek analysis of federal crash records found 45 pedestrians age 17 or younger died on Halloween from 2010 to 2024, with most fatalities occurring during early evening trick-or-treating hours. Mental Health Minnesota Opioid Deaths Fall for Third Year, but Overdose Deaths Rise 3% Minnesota reported 1,025 drug overdose deaths in 2025, up 3% from 2024, as declining opioid fatalities were offset by increases involving methamphetamine and cocaine. California Psychiatric Nurse Ratios Have Cost Nearly 70 Beds Since June, Mental Health Groups Warn State Health and advocacy groups say California has lost nearly 70 psychiatric beds since June after new nurse ratios took effect, intensifying concerns about access and hospital costs. An 85-Year-Old Saw Smoke Coming From His Bed, and a Stray Cat's Scratch Was the Likely Cause An 85-year-old man in China developed high fever, hallucinations, confusion and a collapse months after a stray cat scratched him. Conditions Stanislaus County Mpox: Two Clade I Cases Confirmed as Three of Four Patients Had No Travel Abroad Published Oct 31, 2026 8:40 AM EDT By Dorothy Brooks KENA BETANCUR | AFP via Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on WhatsApp Stanislaus County health officials have identified four recent mpox cases, and California state health officials have confirmed that two of them are clade I, the type of mpox that has historically caused more severe illness. Three of the four people had not traveled outside the country, the Modesto Bee reported on Oct. 29. Testing has not yet classified the other two cases, and officials are still looking into the fourth person's travel history. One person was hospitalized. The lack of travel is the key detail for Modesto-area residents. Clade I cases in the U.S. were long tied to travel abroad, so infections in people who have not left the country raise concern that the virus is spreading locally. Still, county officials say the risk to the general public is low. A Local Signal of Wider Spread Dr. Thea Papasozomenos, Stanislaus County's public health officer, said the "risk to the general public remains low." The Stanislaus cases fit a national pattern. Since August, a growing share of U.S. clade I cases have occurred in people with no recent international travel and no known link to a traveler, according to the CDC's clade I mpox situation summary. The agency says presumed domestic spread has been reported in more than 10 jurisdictions, which it calls a sign of a "likely transition to sustained clade Ib transmission in the United States." As of Oct. 14, the CDC counted more than 90 clade I cases in at least 23 states and Puerto Rico. The Modesto Bee has since reported almost 130 cases in 26 states and Puerto Rico. California saw this pattern first. In October 2025, state officials confirmed three unrelated clade I cases in Southern California, in Long Beach and Los Angeles County, among people who had not traveled internationally or had contact with one another. They were the first U.S. clade I cases not linked to travel. All three patients were hospitalized and were recovering with standard medical care, according to a California Department of Public Health health advisory. MedicalDaily previously reported that California issued a June health alert on rising clade I introductions. At that time, all seven of the state's 2026 clade I cases were linked to travel. The Stanislaus cases suggest that has changed. Clade I Compared With the 2022 Strain The 2022 global outbreak was driven by clade II, which mostly caused milder illness and spread largely through sexual networks among men who have sex with men. Clade I has historically caused more severe disease and has also spread through household contact in parts of Africa, including among children. Severity estimates vary. Recent cases outside Africa have been milder. The CDC says travel-associated clade I cases in the U.S. have been almost entirely clade Ib, with no deaths and relatively mild illness in the available data, and that more than 300 clade Ib cases reported in high-income countries have resulted in no deaths. State health officials have also said clade I has not been shown to spread more easily than clade II. People with weakened immune systems, including those with poorly controlled HIV, face a higher risk of severe disease. Public reports have not described the patients' ages, how they were infected, or whether the Stanislaus cases are connected to each other or to cases elsewhere in California. Vaccine Eligibility for Higher-Risk Residents The CDC rates the risk to the general U.S. population as low and the risk to men who have sex with men as low to moderate. For most Modesto-area households, that means no change in routine is needed. People in higher-risk groups, however, can protect themselves with vaccination. Mpox spreads mainly through close skin-to-skin contact, including sex, and can also spread through shared bedding, towels, or clothing. Casual contact is not known to spread it easily. The California Department of Public Health recommends the two-dose JYNNEOS vaccine for gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men; transgender, nonbinary, and gender-diverse people; people with HIV or those taking HIV PrEP or doxy-PEP; and anyone exposed to mpox in the past two weeks. It is also recommended for travelers to countries where clade I is spreading who expect sexual or intimate contact there. The doses are given four weeks apart, and people who received only one dose should complete the series. JYNNEOS is expected to protect against both clade I and clade II. When Los Angeles County confirmed its locally acquired clade I case last year, health officer Dr. Muntu Davis said, "The identification of cases of clade I mpox, which may cause more severe illness than the more common clade II is concerning," LAist reported. The county urged people at high risk to get the two-dose vaccine. Stanislaus County has dealt with mpox before. The county's case count climbed to 22 during the 2022 outbreak, and the Health Services Agency added vaccination clinics in response. Residents with questions about vaccine access can call the Stanislaus County Immunization Clinic at 209-558-7700 or ask their health care provider. Symptoms and When to Seek Care Symptoms include a painful or itchy rash or sores, fever, chills, swollen lymph nodes, headache, body aches, and fatigue. Some people develop only a few sores, which can be mistaken for other infections. Anyone with a new, unexplained rash or sores should contact a health care provider about testing, which involves swabbing the sores, and avoid close contact with others until evaluated. People diagnosed with mpox should follow medical guidance and stay isolated until all sores have healed and new skin has formed. Covering sores and not sharing bedding or towels can help protect household members. People with weakened immune systems should seek care promptly if symptoms appear. Stanislaus County is working with the state to classify the remaining cases, and MedicalDaily will report any additional confirmed infections. news.content: FOX40 News Health officials confirm 4 mpox cases in Stanislaus County Natalie Sierra 2 days ago (FOX40.COM) — Officials with the Stanislaus County Public Health are reporting four confirmed cases of mpox, also known as monkeypox, in the area. The California Department of Public Health confirmed that two of the cases are Clade I, while the other two are still being tested. Three of the people reported that they did not travel internationally, and the travel history for the fourth person is still being assessed. “Historically, Clade I mpox cases in the U.S. were linked to international travel. However, since August 2026, more cases have been reported among people without recent international travel,” health officials said. According to officials, the recently confirmed cases of mpox having no history of international travel suggest that the virus may now be spreading within U.S. communities. The Stanislaus County Health Services Agency is working with CDPH to monitor mpox activity and prevent further spread. Officials assure community members that the risk of contracting the infection remains low, however, they should be familiar with the symptoms as a precaution. “While we have identified four cases in our county, we want residents to know that the risk to the general public remains low,” Dr. Thea Papasozomenos, Stanislaus County Public Health officer, said. “Being aware of the symptoms, getting vaccinated if at risk of exposure to mpox, and seeking medical care when needed are important ways to protect yourself and prevent the spread of mpox.” Mpox, a viral infection, causes painful or itchy rashes and flu-like symptoms: A rash or sores that may look like pimples or blisters Fever, chills, or swollen lymph nodes Headache, muscle aches, or fatigue The two main types are Clade I and Clade II, which both spread through close, personal contact with someone infected. This includes skin-to-skin contact, intimate or sexual contact and contact with infected sores or bodily fluids. “It can also spread through shared items such as bedding, towels, or clothing that have been contaminated with the virus,” officials said. Prevention methods include the JYNNEOS vaccine for people at increased risk of mpox exposure and avoiding close contact with anyone who has an unexplained rash or sores. More information on mpox can be found here. More information on vaccines can be found here. Ad Your Privacy Choices

analysis_en.event: Two of the cases are confirmed as Clade I, while the other two are still being tested. The cases are reported by the Stanislaus County Public Health and the California Department of Public Health.

news.source_body_en: Health officials in Stanislaus County, California, confirmed four cases of mpox on October 30, 2026. Two of the cases were identified as Clade I, while the other two are still under testing. Three of the individuals involved in the cases reported no international travel, and the travel history of the fourth is being assessed. Officials noted that the risk to the general public remains low, but they urged residents to be aware of symptoms and take preventive measures. The Stanislaus County Health Services Agency is working with the California Department of Public Health to monitor the situation and prevent further spread. Prevention methods include the JYNNEOS vaccine for those at higher risk and avoiding close contact with anyone showing signs of mpox. The cases highlight a trend of mpox spreading among people without recent international travel, which has been observed since August 2026.

news.content: Feedback RSS Feed Sitemap Home Odisha Nation World Sports Business Entertainment Videos Science & Tech Photo Gallery Odisha Special No Result View All Result Home Odisha Nation World Sports Business Entertainment Videos Science & Tech Photo Gallery Odisha Special No Result View All Result Home World Pakistan: Four New Mpox Cases Reported In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa by OMMCOM NEWS October 28, 2026 in World Islamabad: Four new cases of mpox have been reported in Pakistan’s northwest Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, bringing the total number of infections in the province to 18, the provincial health department said on Tuesday. Peshawar, the provincial capital, has reported the highest number of cases, with five infections, while one death from the disease has been recorded so far, the department said, Xinhua News Agency reported. Symptoms of mpox include fever, headache, body aches and skin rashes or blisters. The department advised people to avoid close contact with infected individuals to reduce the risk of transmission. Last month, a case of monkeypox was confirmed in Pakistan’s southern port city of Karachi in Sindh province, the provincial health department said. According to hospital officials, a 45-year-old resident of Karachi’s Surjani town tested positive for the virus through a PCR test after developing a rash. The patient was brought to the Sindh Infectious Diseases Hospital and was undergoing treatment at the facility, officials had said. The latest case increased the number of confirmed monkeypox infections in Sindh province to 42 this year, including 14 cases reported in Karachi, according to the provincial health department. Authorities were conducting surveillance and monitoring efforts to prevent further spread of the disease. Mpox, previously known as monkeypox, is a viral disease caused by an orthopoxvirus called monkeypox virus and spreads primarily through close contact with someone who has mpox, causing a painful rash, enlarged lymph nodes and fever. It can make people very sick and leave scars. The disease mainly spreads from person to person through close contact, according to the World Health Organization (WHO) statement. Transmission occurs through exposure to bodily fluids; lesions on the skin or on internal mucosal surfaces, such as in the mouth or throat; respiratory particles; and contaminated objects. Prevention and control of mpox rely on raising awareness in communities and educating health workers to prevent infection and stop transmission. WHO recommends the use of vaccines for those most at risk of exposure during outbreaks, including people who have had close contact with someone with mpox, and health workers. People who were vaccinated against smallpox in childhood may have some cross-protection against mpox. news.content_original: Feedback RSS Feed Sitemap Home Odisha Nation World Sports Business Entertainment Videos Science & Tech Photo Gallery Odisha Special No Result View All Result Home Odisha Nation World Sports Business Entertainment Videos Science & Tech Photo Gallery Odisha Special No Result View All Result Home World Pakistan: Four New Mpox Cases Reported In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa by OMMCOM NEWS October 28, 2026 in World Islamabad: Four new cases of mpox have been reported in Pakistan’s northwest Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, bringing the total number of infections in the province to 18, the provincial health department said on Tuesday. Peshawar, the provincial capital, has reported the highest number of cases, with five infections, while one death from the disease has been recorded so far, the department said, Xinhua News Agency reported. Symptoms of mpox include fever, headache, body aches and skin rashes or blisters. The department advised people to avoid close contact with infected individuals to reduce the risk of transmission. Last month, a case of monkeypox was confirmed in Pakistan’s southern port city of Karachi in Sindh province, the provincial health department said. According to hospital officials, a 45-year-old resident of Karachi’s Surjani town tested positive for the virus through a PCR test after developing a rash. The patient was brought to the Sindh Infectious Diseases Hospital and was undergoing treatment at the facility, officials had said. The latest case increased the number of confirmed monkeypox infections in Sindh province to 42 this year, including 14 cases reported in Karachi, according to the provincial health department. Authorities were conducting surveillance and monitoring efforts to prevent further spread of the disease. Mpox, previously known as monkeypox, is a viral disease caused by an orthopoxvirus called monkeypox virus and spreads primarily through close contact with someone who has mpox, causing a painful rash, enlarged lymph nodes and fever. It can make people very sick and leave scars. The disease mainly spreads from person to person through close contact, according to the World Health Organization (WHO) statement. Transmission occurs through exposure to bodily fluids; lesions on the skin or on internal mucosal surfaces, such as in the mouth or throat; respiratory particles; and contaminated objects. Prevention and control of mpox rely on raising awareness in communities and educating health workers to prevent infection and stop transmission. WHO recommends the use of vaccines for those most at risk of exposure during outbreaks, including people who have had close contact with someone with mpox, and health workers. People who were vaccinated against smallpox in childhood may have some cross-protection against mpox. Pakistan: Four New Mpox Cases Surface in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Total Reaches 18 Four new mpox cases have been reported in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, bringing the total number of infections there to 18. The provincial health department confirmed the new cases, highlighting an ongoing public health concern. Peshawar, the provincial capital, has recorded the highest number of cases, with five infections. Tragically, one death related to mpox has also been reported in the province. Symptoms associated with mpox include fever, headache, body aches, and characteristic skin rashes or blisters. Health officials are advising residents to maintain distance from infected individuals to curb further transmission. Separately, in Pakistan's southern port city of Karachi, Sindh province, authorities have confirmed 42 mpox infections this year, with 14 cases originating from Karachi itself. A recent case involved a 45-year-old Karachi resident who tested positive after developing a rash and is currently receiving treatment at the Sindh Infectious Diseases Hospital. Health departments across Pakistan are actively monitoring the situation and implementing surveillance measures to prevent a wider spread of the disease. Mpox, previously known as monkeypox, is a viral illness caused by the monkeypox virus. It primarily spreads through close contact, leading to painful rashes, enlarged lymph nodes, and fever. The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes community awareness and health worker education as key prevention strategies. Vaccination is recommended for those at high risk, including close contacts of infected individuals and healthcare workers. news.content: Scoop has an Ethical Paywall Licence needed for work use Start Free Trial  World  Contact  About  ScoopPro  Scoop Werewolf Wellington The Dig Business Scoop Pacific Community Review of Books InfoPages Front Page Scoops Parliament Politics Regional Business Sci-Tech World Culture Education Health    Contact  About  ScoopPro Scoop Front Page Scoops Parliament Politics Regional Business Sci-Tech World Culture Education Health Network Scoop Werewolf Wellington Scoop The Dig Business Scoop Pacific Community Review of Books InfoPages World Video | Defence | Foreign Affairs | Natural Events | Trade | NZ in World News | NZ National News Video | NZ Regional News | Search Scoop  World   A New Report From The Independent Panel - Hiding In Plain Sight: Mpox And The Cost Of Neglecting Known Threats Saturday, 31 October 2026, 3:34 pm Press Release: The Independent Panel A new report from The Independent Panel for Pandemic Preparedness and Response traces how mpox, once a sporadic disease in West and Central Africa mainly caused by contact with infected animals, is now causing outbreaks in dozens of countries around the world and counts humans as a reservoir. The Independent Panel’s latest report – Hiding in Plain Sight: Mpox and the Cost of Neglecting Known Threats – finds that the long-term neglect of mpox contributed to two preventable global health emergencies and made the disease a widespread public health risk. The report also shows how new variants of the monkeypox virus have emerged over a relatively short period of time, adding risks to people and burdens on already stretched health systems. “We must stop ignoring sporadic diseases with epidemic potential,” said the Right Honourable Helen Clark, Co-Chair of The Independent Panel. “Mpox was neglected at our peril. Preventable health emergencies are a sign of failure. They happen when community health care is neglected, signals are missed, and pathogens are allowed to spread beyond their original habitats. These gaps leave us all vulnerable.” Mpox is nowhere near as dangerous as smallpox, caused by the related variola virus, but it causes painful lesions that last weeks, may require hospitalisation, is more dangerous for people with advanced or untreated HIV, and has caused foetal and child deaths. “There were earlier opportunities to control mpox, which was primarily a zoonotic illness in endemic countries in West and Central Africa,” said the report’s lead author, Dr Els Torreele. Advertisement - scroll to continue reading “With 145 countries reporting mpox in the last four years and many outbreaks of sustained human-to-human transmission, the opportunity to stop it locally was missed. We are all paying a price with a disease that now counts humans as a reservoir.” The right tools were not in the right place at the right time The report documents that prior to 2022, smallpox vaccines and treatments with potential against mpox existed because of health security investments and biodefence research. However, these were first used widely to support mpox control during the 2022 global emergency, when high-income countries were also affected. This was an opportunity to document the vaccine’s efficacy against mpox, but it was still not made available in the original endemic regions – particularly in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which had been reporting around 2,000 suspected cases each year. Vaccines against mpox were deployed on the African continent only after the emergence of a new viral subtype, a cross-border surge and the declaration of a second public health emergency of international concern in August 2024. When finally available, vaccines were provided to several countries experiencing outbreaks in a staggered manner. Ultimately, it is unclear how much impact they had on the 2024–2025 mpox outbreaks. An mpox vaccine stockpile was announced only in August 2026. Further, tools like rapid diagnostic tests and therapies were not available where they were most needed. Only about one-third of suspected cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo could be confirmed with testing “Many of the lessons of mpox are similar to those from the COVID-19 experience,” said Dr Joanne Liu, a member of The Independent Panel. “Tools like vaccines were not prioritised for the people who needed them most. And the one tool that would have made the biggest difference – an affordable, rapid diagnostic test that could be used in communities – still does not exist.” Lessons must be applied and not only learned Lessons from mpox are being relearned in 2026, Independent Panel Co-Chairs Helen Clark and Ellen Johnson Sirleaf write in the report’s foreword. “The Ebola Bundibugyo virus has caused two prior outbreaks in this century. Yet it too surprised the world in 2026, and communities affected were stranded with no near point-of-care tests, no vaccines, no treatments, and eroded trust in government and institutions. A world that cannot manage known diseases will not be ready for Disease X, the next pandemic threat.” Mpox is now global The consequences are still unfolding. In 2026, 82 countries have confirmed more than 14,000 cases. Madagascar, which had never previously recorded an mpox case, now faces the world’s largest outbreak of 2026 with more than 3,400 cases and 22 deaths as of mid-August. In the EU/EEA in the last 12 months, almost 3,800 confirmed mpox cases were reported, and among people with known travel history, most had not travelled, indicating local transmission. People continue to be affected in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where health workers must manage multiple health challenges, including Ebola. Focus on community systems to avoid emergencies "Instead of parachuting in emergency funds for community engagement, leaving behind posters that fade on clinic walls, communities must be supported through sustained investment that builds lasting resilience.” said Dr Torreele. “A response should not only be evaluated through numbers of cases, countries affected, or doses of vaccines deployed, but also by how it leaves communities at risk better prepared and able to stay healthy.” The report is the result of a review of literature and in-depth conversations with people directly involved in the two mpox emergencies and in ongoing mpox research. The lessons explained in the report are considered in the context of the main recommendations of The Independent Panel to address gaps in pandemic prevention, preparedness, and response as set out in its 2021 report, COVID-19: Make it the Last Pandemic. © Scoop Media Using Scoop for work?
